\n <div><h2>Как это работает</h2>\n:
How it works

At rest the inside of a neuron is at about −70 mV. This charge is maintained by the Na⁺/K⁺ pump and potassium leak channels.

Signals from the dendrites summate on the cell body. If the charge at the axon hillock reaches threshold (about −55…−50 mV), fast Na⁺ channels open and an action potential fires: sodium rushes in, the charge shoots up to +30 mV, then potassium flows out and restores the negative charge.

Why myelin

Myelin is insulation made by glial cells. The channels are clustered at the nodes of Ranvier, and the impulse jumps from node to node. Turn myelin off and the impulse will creep along as a continuous wave, several times slower.

Local anesthesia

Lidocaine and procaine plug Na⁺ channels. In the treated segment the impulse dies out, and the pain signal never reaches the brain.

  • The order of events: summation, hillock, Na⁺ influx, K⁺ efflux.
  • Saltatory conduction and sodium channel block.

\n <div><h2>Зачем нейронам глия</h2:
Why neurons need glia

Glia were described and named “neuroglia” by Rudolf Virchow (1856); the shapes of glial cells were revealed by Golgi and Ramón y Cajal. Glia fill all the space between neurons. Across the whole brain there are roughly as many glial cells as neurons (~1:1). In the cortical gray matter there are about 1.5 glial cells per neuron, in the brainstem up to ten, while in the cerebellum, packed with tiny granule cells, glia are several times fewer than neurons. Gliocytes are 3–4 times smaller than neurons, contain little Nissl substance, form no synapses and do not transmit signals electrically.

Blood–brain barrier

The barrier itself is the capillary endothelium: its cells are sealed by tight junctions, and substances from the blood enter the brain only through transporters. Astrocyte end feet sheathe almost the entire capillary and support the barrier. Glutamate is the main excitatory neurotransmitter and one of the most common amino acids in food, but gut cells burn almost all dietary glutamate, and plasma glutamate crosses the barrier poorly. That is why a protein meal does not overexcite the brain. Turn off “BBB” and see what happens to the neurons.

White and gray matter

Myelin is 75% lipid, with a lot of cholesterol, and is therefore white. Bundles of myelinated axons form the white matter, the “wiring”. The cell bodies and dendrites of neurons form the gray matter. In multiple sclerosis the immune system attacks myelin protein. Myelination proceeds over the first 20 years of life, from the spinal cord to the cortex, and the corpus callosum begins it only in the second month after birth.

Where glia come from

Astrocytes, oligodendrocytes and ependymal cells develop from the neuroectoderm. Microglia are mesodermal: during embryogenesis phagocyte precursor cells enter the brain and stay there.

\n <div><h2>Промежуточный мозг</h2>:
The diencephalon

It develops from the forebrain vesicle: the lower wall gives rise to the hypothalamus (the most ancient part), the side walls to the thalamus, the upper wall to the epithalamus with the pineal gland, and the back wall to the metathalamus (the geniculate bodies). All these structures grew from the alar (dorsal) plate of the neural tube, so they contain no motor neurons, only relay neurons and interneurons.

Thalamus

Neuroanatomists distinguish about 40 nuclei, neurosurgeons up to 80. Specific nuclei pass sensory and motor signals to the cortex with a precise map of the body, the retina or the cochlea. Nonspecific nuclei set the overall tone of the cortex and work in the sleep–wake system. Association nuclei (the pulvinar, the dorsal nuclei) are connected with the frontal and parietal cortex and help recognize complex images. In chronic pain, neurosurgeons make precise lesions in certain thalamic networks.

Hypothalamus

The anterior nuclei produce parasympathetic effects (slowing of the heart, constriction of the pupil), the posterior nuclei sympathetic ones (dilation of the pupil, a rise in blood pressure). The medial zones handle the motivation to eat and drink, the anterior zones sexual and parental behavior, the posterior zones fear and aggression. The suprachiasmatic nuclei are the biological clock.

The telencephalon

The largest part of the brain, it covers all the others, and the longitudinal fissure divides it into two hemispheres. On the outside is the cortex with its sulci and gyri, beneath it the white matter, and deep inside the basal ganglia: the caudate nucleus, putamen, globus pallidus, claustrum and amygdala.

What the parts are called

Putamen + globus pallidus = lentiform nucleus. Caudate + lentiform = corpus striatum (the classical anatomical term). In the modern sense the striatum is the caudate + putamen (dorsal striatum) and the nucleus accumbens (ventral striatum); the globus pallidus is not part of it but a separate stage of the basal ganglia.

Basal ganglia and cerebellum

The cerebellum remembers how to perform a particular movement quickly and precisely (a single step in a dance). The basal ganglia assemble movements into a long program (the whole dance with its transitions between figures). In both cases synaptic plasticity is at work.

\n <div><h2>Борозды и извилины</h2>:
Sulci and gyri

The primary sulci (central, lateral, parieto-occipital) appear from the 5th month of fetal development and are present in everyone. Secondary sulci come later. Tertiary sulci produce fine furrowing, and their pattern is individual.

Cortical areas are not equal

Primary areas are the cortical stations of the sensory systems, with direct input from the thalamic relay nuclei and a precise topographic map. Secondary areas lie next to the primary ones, are connected with the association nuclei and assemble features into images. Tertiary areas — the inferior parietal lobule and the occipito-temporo-parietal region — combine different streams.

In sensory systems an image is assembled from elements; in motor systems the flow runs the other way: overall program (prefrontal cortex) → individual movements (6, 8) → signals to the muscles (4).

Cortical cells

  • Pyramidal cells — 3/4 of cortical neurons, with many dendritic spines (a sign of learning).
  • Betz cells — the largest neurons in the brain (V. A. Betz, 1874), in layer V of the precentral gyrus; their axons go into the pyramidal tract.
  • Von Economo neurons — large spindle-shaped cells found only in humans, great apes, elephants and cetaceans: fast communication between the frontal, parietal and cingulate cortex.
  • Long-axon Golgi type I cells project beyond the cortex; short-axon Golgi type II cells form local networks.

\n <div><h2>Как работает насос</h2>:
How the pump works

In diastole, blood from the veins flows freely through the open atrioventricular valves into the ventricles. Atrial systole pushes in the last 20–30%. In ventricular systole the pressure rises, the atrioventricular valve cusps snap shut (first heart sound, “lub”), the semilunar valves open, and blood leaves into the aorta and pulmonary trunk. When the ventricles relax, the semilunar valves close (second heart sound, “dub”).

Stroke volume and cardiac output

With each contraction, each ventricle ejects about 70 mL. At 70 beats per minute that is ~5 L/min; during exercise, up to 25–30 L/min.

Regulation

  • Sympathetic nerves and epinephrine (adrenaline) increase the rate and force of contraction.
  • The vagus nerve (parasympathetic) slows the rhythm.
  • The more the ventricle is stretched by incoming blood, the more forcefully it contracts (the Frank–Starling law).

Loudness and frequency

The ear codes frequency by the place on the membrane (high frequencies near the base) and, for low sounds, by the rhythm of impulses. Loudness is coded by the number of active fibers and their firing rate. The range of loudness is enormous: from 0 dB (threshold of hearing) to 120–130 dB (threshold of pain).

Why hearing declines

Hair cells do not regenerate. Loud music and noise damage them; the cells at the base suffer first — so high frequencies are lost first.

Germ cells

The egg (~0.1 mm) is the largest cell in the body; the sperm (~0.05 mm including the tail) is one of the smallest. Both are formed by meiosis and carry 23 chromosomes each. The sex of the child is determined by the sperm: one with an X chromosome gives a girl (XX), one with a Y gives a boy (XY).

Hormonal regulation

Hypothalamus (GnRH) → pituitary (FSH and LH) → ovaries or testes (estrogens, progesterone, testosterone), which act back on the hypothalamus and pituitary through feedback.

Phases of the cycle

Menstrual phase (days 1–5): progesterone has fallen, and the functional layer of the endometrium is shed. Follicular phase (until about day 14): under FSH the follicles grow, the dominant one secretes more and more estradiol, and the endometrium thickens again. When estradiol stays high for about two days, the feedback switches to positive: the pituitary releases an LH surge, and about 36 hours later ovulation occurs. The luteal phase is nearly constant (~14 days): the corpus luteum secretes progesterone and estradiol, and the endometrium prepares for implantation; without pregnancy the corpus luteum regresses, hormone levels fall, and a new menstruation begins. That is why cycle length (21–35 days) varies mainly through the follicular phase.

\n <div><h2>Ферменты</h2>\n:
Enzymes

Enzymes are biological catalysts made of protein. Three properties set them apart from other catalysts: enormous efficiency, strict specificity and the capacity for regulation.

Simple enzymes consist of protein only (pepsin, amylase, lipase). Conjugated enzymes consist of a protein part (the apoenzyme) and a non-protein cofactor: either tightly bound — a prosthetic group (metal ions, heme) — or an easily detached coenzyme (most often a vitamin derivative). Together they form the holoenzyme.

How an enzyme speeds up a reaction

An enzyme does not change the energy of the starting materials or products, but it lowers the activation energy — the barrier that must be overcome (graph on the right). Mechanisms: precise orientation of the substrate (binding at a minimum of three points), strain on its bonds, acid–base catalysis (like Glu35 and Asp52 of lysozyme, or the histidine of many enzymes) and covalent catalysis.

Michaelis–Menten stages: E + S ⇄ ES → ES* → EP → E + P.

Specificity

  • Absolute — a single substrate (arginase → arginine only).
  • Relative — a group of similar substrates (lipase — all fats, pepsin — proteins).
  • Stereospecificity — only one isomer (L- or D-).
  • Reaction specificity: from histidine, histidase makes a keto acid, while a decarboxylase makes histamine.

\n <div><h2>От чего зависит скорост:
What the rate depends on

Substrate concentration. At low [S] the rate rises almost linearly; at high [S] it levels off at Vmax: all enzymes are occupied (saturation). Km equals the [S] at which v = ½ Vmax; it is inversely related to the enzyme’s affinity for the substrate.

Temperature. Up to the optimum (~37–40 °C) the rate roughly doubles for every 10 °C; above 45–50 °C the protein denatures (thermolability).

pH. Each enzyme has its own optimum: pepsin works in the acidic stomach (pH 1.5–2), trypsin in the slightly alkaline intestine (~8). When gastric juice is not acidic enough, pepsin digests proteins poorly.

Enzyme concentration — the rate is directly proportional to it. Units of activity: 1 IU = 1 µmol of substrate per 1 min; 1 katal = 1 mol per 1 s.

Inhibitors

Reversible inhibitors bind by weak bonds: competitive (substrate analogs, ↑Km) and noncompetitive (bind elsewhere, ↓Vmax). Irreversible inhibitors form a covalent bond — they are often poisons. In Lineweaver–Burk coordinates (1/v vs 1/[S]) the curve becomes a straight line: a competitive inhibitor changes its slope but not its intercept on the 1/v axis, while a noncompetitive inhibitor raises that intercept.

  • Partial proteolysis — proenzyme → enzyme (irreversible).
  • Phosphorylation / dephosphorylation — protein kinases and phosphatases, fast and reversible.

Enzymes in medicine

Enzymopathies are inherited diseases caused by a defective enzyme (phenylketonuria, galactosemia). Enzyme therapy uses enzymes and their inhibitors as drugs: pancreatic enzymes for pancreatic insufficiency, protease inhibitors for pancreatitis. Enzyme diagnostics measures blood enzymes (ALT, AST, CK-MB, amylase, LDH, alkaline phosphatase) and uses pure enzymes as reagents to measure glucose, cholesterol and urea.

What vitamins are

Water-soluble vitamins (the B group and C) are not stored (except B12), so they must be obtained constantly. Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) are absorbed together with fats and stored in the liver and adipose tissue — so an overdose is possible (hypervitaminosis A and D).

Avitaminosis is a complete absence, hypovitaminosis a deficiency, hypervitaminosis an excess. Causes: a poor diet, impaired absorption, increased need (pregnancy, growth), suppression of the gut flora by antibiotics, and antivitamins — competing substances (methotrexate against B9, warfarin against K, avidin against biotin, isoniazid against B6).

\n <div><h2>Энергия в клетке</h2>\n:
Energy in the cell

Metabolism = catabolism (breakdown, ΔG < 0, exergonic reactions) + anabolism (synthesis, ΔG > 0, endergonic). They are linked by coupling: the energy of breakdown is stored in high-energy compounds (ATP) and reduced coenzymes (NADH, NADPH, FADH₂) and spent on synthesis and work.

Change in free energy: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. If ΔG < 0, the reaction proceeds spontaneously; if ΔG > 0, only when paired with an energy-yielding reaction.

How ATP is made

Oxidative phosphorylation (mitochondria, ~90%) and substrate-level phosphorylation (glycolysis, Krebs cycle). Muscles have a fast reserve — creatine phosphate: creatine kinase transfers its phosphate to ADP in a fraction of a second.

Stages of metabolism

  1. Intake with food.
  2. Digestion to monomers.
  3. Absorption and transport in blood and lymph.
  4. Intermediary metabolism in cells.
  5. Excretion of end products: CO₂, H₂O, urea.

\n <div><h2>Итог цикла</h2>\n:
Net result of the cycle

Acetyl-CoA + 3 NAD⁺ + FAD + GDP + Pi + 2 H₂O → 2 CO₂ + 3 NADH + FADH₂ + GTP + HS-CoA.

Eight hydrogen atoms (4 pairs) go to the respiratory chain and end up as water, and their energy ends up in ATP. The cycle itself does not use oxygen, but without oxygen it stops: NAD⁺ and FAD are not regenerated.

The cycle as a crossroads

The cycle is amphibolic: its intermediates are drawn off for synthesis (citrate → fatty acids and cholesterol, α-ketoglutarate → glutamate, succinyl-CoA → heme, oxaloacetate → aspartate and glucose). Losses are replenished by anaplerotic reactions, chiefly pyruvate carboxylase (with biotin): pyruvate + CO₂ → oxaloacetate.

Energy

Using textbook values (P/O = 3 for NADH and 2 for FADH₂), oxidation of 1 acetyl-CoA yields 12 ATP, and of glucose 38 ATP. Modern measurements give ≈ 2.5 and 1.5 ATP — that is, about 10 ATP per turn and 30–32 per glucose.

\n <div><h2>Окислительное фосфорили:

They are arranged in order of increasing redox potential: from NAD⁺/NADH (−0.32 V) to O₂/H₂O (+0.82 V).

Coupling of respiration to phosphorylation is provided by the proton gradient (ΔpH + membrane potential ≈ 0.2 V). The P/O ratio is the number of ATP formed per oxygen atom: 3 for NADH and 2 for FADH₂ in textbooks, ≈ 2.5 and 1.5 by current data.

Routes of oxygen consumption

~90% of O₂ goes to the respiratory chain. The rest goes to monooxygenases (liver cytochrome P450), oxidases and, unfortunately, electron leakage that forms reactive oxygen species (superoxide, H₂O₂), which are neutralized by superoxide dismutase, catalase and glutathione peroxidase.

\n <div><h2>Пути глюкозы</h2>\n:
Pathways of glucose

The dichotomous pathway (glycolysis): glucose → 2 pyruvate. Without oxygen — 2 lactate and 2 ATP; with oxygen — CO₂ and H₂O, 38 ATP (textbook value). The apotomic pathway (pentose phosphate) is direct oxidation producing NADPH and pentoses.

Three reactions are irreversible: the hexokinase (1), phosphofructokinase (3) and pyruvate kinase (10) reactions. Their enzymes are regulatory, and in gluconeogenesis they are replaced by bypass enzymes (I–IV).

Cori cycle

During intense work, muscle releases lactate into the blood; the liver turns it back into glucose and returns it to the muscle. The liver gets the energy for this (6 ATP) from fat oxidation.

Other sugars

Fructose and galactose enter glycolysis via their own enzymes. Inherited galactosemia (a defect of galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase) causes cataracts and liver and brain damage in infants; it is treated with a milk-free diet.

The liver holds about 100–120 g of glycogen (up to 6% of its mass); it lasts for 12–24 hours of fasting and serves the whole body. Muscles hold 300–400 g (1–2%), but only “for themselves”: muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase.

Regulation

Insulin activates glycogen synthase and inhibits phosphorylase (via phosphatases). Glucagon (liver) and epinephrine (liver and muscle) trigger a cascade: receptor → G protein → adenylate cyclase → cAMP → protein kinase A → phosphorylase kinase → phosphorylase. Phosphorylation switches phosphorylase on and at the same time switches glycogen synthase off. In muscle, breakdown is also accelerated by the Ca²⁺ of contraction and by AMP.

Inherited defects of the breakdown enzymes: von Gierke disease (glucose-6-phosphatase — hypoglycemia, enlarged liver), Pompe disease (lysosomal α-glucosidase — heart involvement), McArdle disease (muscle phosphorylase — cramps during exercise). Aglycogenoses are defects of synthesis.

Synthesis: 2 acetyl-CoA → acetoacetyl-CoA → HMG-CoA → acetoacetate → β-hydroxybutyrate (by reduction) or acetone (spontaneously). Use in tissues: acetoacetate + succinyl-CoA → acetoacetyl-CoA → 2 acetyl-CoA → Krebs cycle. Carnitine deficiency (in premature infants, on hemodialysis) — muscle weakness, hypoglycemia. Inherited defects of acyl-CoA dehydrogenases. Obesity — lipogenesis outweighing lipolysis.

Normal total cholesterol is about 5.2 ± 1.3 mmol/L (recommended: below 5.2), LDL below 3, HDL above 1.0 in men and 1.2 in women, TAG below 1.7. Familial hypercholesterolemia is an inherited defect of the LDL receptor: cholesterol is 2–6 times above normal, and heart attacks occur at a young age.

\n <div><h2>Липогенез</h2>\n:
Lipogenesis

The fatty acids in fat come from food or are synthesized from acetyl-CoA (excess carbohydrate) in the liver and adipose tissue. Synthesis is switched on by insulin and excess glucose and inhibited by glucagon and epinephrine.

Obesity

Body mass index = weight (kg) / height² (m²): 18.5–25 is normal, 25–30 overweight, ≥ 30 obesity. Where the fat is stored also matters: visceral fat (around the organs) is more dangerous than subcutaneous fat. Adipose tissue is an endocrine organ: leptin tells the brain about the energy stores (in obesity there is plenty of it, but the brain becomes insensitive to it), and adiponectin increases insulin sensitivity (in obesity it is low).

Fatty liver

Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD; since 2023 renamed metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, MASLD) is the most common liver disease in the world; it is linked to obesity and insulin resistance.

\n <div><h2>Азотистый баланс</h2>\n:
Nitrogen balance

The body’s proteins are constantly being renewed (~300 g a day). Nitrogen balance is the difference between the nitrogen taken in with food and the nitrogen excreted: it is positive in growing children and pregnant women, and negative in starvation, burns and severe illness. The protein requirement of an adult is about 1 g per kg of body weight.

Ammonia

NH₃ is highly toxic to the brain (it ties up α-ketoglutarate and disrupts the Krebs cycle in neurons). It is transported in safe forms: glutamine (glutamine synthetase) and alanine (the glucose–alanine cycle from muscle). In the kidneys, glutaminase releases NH₃, which leaves in the urine as ammonium salts — this is also a way to excrete acid. In cirrhosis, ammonia is not detoxified, leading to hepatic encephalopathy.

Fate of the carbon skeleton

Glucogenic amino acids yield pyruvate and Krebs cycle intermediates (from which glucose can be made); ketogenic ones (leucine, lysine) yield acetyl-CoA and ketone bodies.

\n <div><h2>Обмен нуклеотидов</h2>\:
Nucleotide metabolism

Dietary nucleoproteins are broken down: in the stomach into proteins and nucleic acids; in the intestine pancreatic DNases and RNases and phosphodiesterases yield nucleotides, and nucleotidases yield nucleosides, which are what gets absorbed. But to synthesize its own nucleic acids the body makes nucleotides almost entirely by itself.

Purines and gout

The purine ring is assembled de novo directly on ribose 5-phosphate (PRPP): its atoms come from glycine, glutamine, aspartate, CO₂ and formyl-THF; the first finished nucleotide is IMP, from which AMP and GMP are made. Breakdown runs IMP → inosine → hypoxanthine → xanthine → uric acid; the last two steps are catalyzed by xanthine oxidase. Humans lack uricase, so uric acid is the end product, and it dissolves poorly: above ~420 µmol/L (≈7 mg/dL) monosodium urate crystals precipitate in the joints — this is gout. Allopurinol (and febuxostat) inhibits xanthine oxidase and lowers uric acid production; the treatment target is below 360 µmol/L. In Lesch–Nyhan syndrome (HGPRT deficiency) purines are not recycled into nucleotides by the salvage pathway, PRPP accumulates and speeds up de novo synthesis — uric acid is massively overproduced, and the child has severe neurological problems and self-injury. Purine and thymidine synthesis depends on folate, which is the basis of antimetabolites: methotrexate blocks DHFR, and 6-mercaptopurine takes the place of purines.

Pyrimidines

The pyrimidine ring is built from carbamoyl phosphate (cytosolic CPS II) and aspartate, and ribose is attached at the end (via orotic acid). Pyrimidines are broken down to soluble β-alanine, CO₂ and NH₃ — which is why pyrimidines have no storage diseases like gout. Hereditary orotic aciduria is a defect in UMP synthesis.

Deoxyribonucleotides

They are formed from ribonucleotides by ribonucleotide reductase (inhibited by the anticancer drug hydroxyurea); the thymidine nucleotide is made by thymidylate synthase with methylene-THF.

\n <div><h2>Как работают антибиотик:
How antibiotics work

Antibiotics hit what bacteria have and humans lack (or have in a different form). Protein synthesis: a 70S ribosome instead of 80S : the 30S subunit is targeted by tetracyclines and aminoglycosides, the 50S subunit by macrolides, chloramphenicol and linezolid. The peptidoglycan cell wall — β-lactams (penicillins, cephalosporins) and vancomycin. DNA gyrase — fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin). Bacterial RNA polymerase — rifampin. Folate synthesis — sulfonamides and trimethoprim.

Bactericidal and bacteriostatic

Bactericidal drugs kill (β-lactams, aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones); bacteriostatic drugs stop growth, and the immune system finishes the job (tetracyclines, macrolides, chloramphenicol).

Resistance mechanisms

  • Enzymes that destroy the drug (β-lactamases, aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes).
  • Target modification (methylation of 23S rRNA — macrolides; mutations in protein S12 — streptomycin).
  • Efflux pumps that expel the drug (tetracyclines) and reduced permeability.
  • Ribosomal protection: the TetM and TetO proteins remove tetracycline from the ribosome.
  • Resistance genes are transferred between bacteria on plasmids.

Antibiotics do not work on viruses: viruses have no ribosomes or cell wall of their own.

\n <div><h2>Мутации</h2>\n <:
Mutations

Gene (point) mutations: base substitutions — transitions and transversions; by their consequences — silent, missense, nonsense; insertions and deletions — with or without a frameshift. Transitions are purine ↔ purine or pyrimidine ↔ pyrimidine, transversions are purine ↔ pyrimidine (HbS is an A → T transversion). There are also mutations in regulatory regions and splice sites (many β⁺-thalassemias). Chromosomal mutations — deletions, duplications, inversions, translocations; genomic mutations — a change in chromosome number (trisomy 21).

Causes and defenses

Replication errors, spontaneous deamination and depurination, UV light (thymine dimers), ionizing radiation, chemical mutagens. Repair: direct reversal, excision repair (base and nucleotide excision — a defect causes xeroderma pigmentosum), mismatch repair (defect — Lynch syndrome). See the “DNA: structure, replication, repair” topic.

\n <div><h2>Два пути сигнала</h2>\n:
Two signaling routes

Hydrophilic hormones (proteins, peptides, catecholamines) act through membrane receptors: ionotropic (channels), metabotropic (via G proteins: Gs activates adenylyl cyclase, Gi inhibits it, Gq activates phospholipase C → IP₃ and Ca²⁺ + DAG), and enzyme receptors (tyrosine kinases, guanylyl cyclase). Second messengers: cAMP, cGMP, Ca²⁺, IP₃, DAG, NO. The response takes seconds to minutes and changes enzyme activity.

Lipophilic hormones (steroids, iodothyronines, calcitriol) enter the cell and act on genes through intracellular receptors: the response takes hours and changes the amount of enzymes.

Hierarchy

Hypothalamus (releasing and inhibiting hormones) → pituitary (tropic hormones: ACTH, TSH, FSH, LH, GH, prolactin) → peripheral glands. Negative feedback: the hormones of the glands inhibit the hypothalamus and pituitary.

The key pair is insulin (the anabolic hormone of the fed state) and glucagon (the catabolic hormone of fasting); their ratio sets the direction of metabolism in the liver. It resembles “starvation amid plenty”: without enough insulin, cells do not get glucose, the liver keeps producing it, and lipolysis and ketogenesis switch on as in starvation — yet blood sugar is high.

\n <div><h2>Гормоны щитовидной желе:
Thyroid hormones

T₄ (thyroxine, 3,5,3′,5′-tetraiodothyronine) and T₃ (3,5,3′-triiodothyronine) are iodinated derivatives of tyrosine. The gland secretes mostly T₄; about 80% of T₃ is formed in tissues by deiodinases D1 and D2. Deiodinase D3 produces inactive reverse T₃ (rT₃). In the blood more than 99% of the hormones are bound to proteins (thyroxine-binding globulin, transthyretin, albumin); only the free fraction is active.

Synthesis

  • Iodide uptake: the sodium–iodide symporter (NIS), secondary active transport.
  • Oxidation of iodine and iodination of the tyrosine residues of thyroglobulin — thyroid peroxidase (TPO), which requires H₂O₂.
  • Coupling: DIT + DIT → T₄; MIT + DIT → T₃.
  • Proteolysis of thyroglobulin in lysosomes releases T₄ and T₃; the iodine from MIT and DIT is recycled.

Action

The nuclear receptors TRα and TRβ, paired with RXR, bind to DNA sites (TREs) and change gene transcription. Effects: higher basal metabolic rate and heat production, increased lipolysis and gluconeogenesis, lower cholesterol, growth and maturation of bone and brain, and stronger effects of catecholamines on the heart.

Tests

TSH (normal about 0.4–4.0 mU/L), free T₄ (about 10–22 pmol/L), antibodies to TPO (Hashimoto’s) and to the TSH receptor (Graves’).

Steroid hormones

All steroids are cholesterol derivatives with four rings (cyclopentanoperhydrophenanthrene). The enzymes of steroidogenesis are mostly cytochromes P450 (CYP11A1, CYP17, CYP21, CYP11B1, CYP11B2) in the mitochondria and ER. Prednisolone and dexamethasone suppress inflammation and immunity (phospholipase A₂, cytokines). Long-term use causes Cushing’s syndrome and suppression of the body’s own adrenal cortex, so they are withdrawn gradually.

\n <div><h2>Обмен кальция и фосфата:
Calcium and phosphate metabolism

The body contains about 1 kg of calcium, 99% of it in bone as hydroxyapatite. Total plasma calcium is 2.2–2.6 mmol/L: almost half is bound to albumin, and the active fraction is ionized calcium (1.1–1.3 mmol/L). Acidosis increases the ionized fraction, alkalosis (for example, with hyperventilation) decreases it — cramps may occur.

Hormones

  • Parathyroid hormone (84 amino acids): bone — resorption via RANKL on osteoblasts; kidneys — Ca²⁺ reabsorption, phosphate excretion, calcitriol synthesis.
  • Calcitriol (1,25-(OH)₂-D₃): nuclear receptor VDR; in the intestine it switches on calcium-absorption proteins (TRPV6, calbindin), acts on bone and kidneys, inhibits PTH.
  • Calcitonin (C cells of the thyroid gland): inhibits osteoclasts.
  • FGF23 from bone promotes phosphate excretion and inhibits calcitriol synthesis.

Diseases

Hyper- and hypoparathyroidism, rickets and osteomalacia, osteoporosis, renal osteodystrophy, hypercalcemia of malignancy (PTH-related peptide, PTHrP).

\n <div><h2>Гипоталамо-гипофизарная:
The hypothalamic–pituitary system

The hypothalamus links the nervous system to the endocrine system. Its parvocellular neurons release releasing and inhibiting hormones into the portal system: thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH), corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH), gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), growth hormone–releasing hormone (GHRH), somatostatin and dopamine (prolactin-inhibiting factor). Magnocellular neurons of the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei synthesize vasopressin and oxytocin together with neurophysin proteins; the hormones are stored in axon terminals in the posterior lobe.

  • Proteins and peptides: GH (191 amino acids), prolactin (199), ACTH (39) — from pro-opiomelanocortin together with MSH and β-endorphin.
  • Glycoproteins of α and β subunits: TSH, LH, FSH (the α subunit is also shared with human chorionic gonadotropin).
  • Feedback: target-gland hormones (cortisol, T₄, sex steroids) and IGF-1 inhibit the hypothalamus and pituitary.

Mechanism of action

TSH, LH, FSH, ACTH, vasopressin (V2) — G protein–coupled receptors (cAMP); vasopressin (V1) and oxytocin — via phospholipase C and Ca²⁺; GH and prolactin — receptors coupled to JAK tyrosine kinases.

  • Pituitary adenomas: prolactinoma, somatotropinoma (gigantism, acromegaly), corticotropinoma (Cushing’s disease); large tumors compress the optic chiasm.
  • Hypopituitarism (for example, after childbirth with heavy blood loss — Sheehan syndrome).
  • Diabetes insipidus (central, nephrogenic), syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion.

\n <div><h2>Инсулин</h2>\n <:
Insulin

A protein of two chains (A — 21 and B — 30 amino acids) joined by two disulfide bridges. It is made as preproinsulin; in the granules C-peptide is cut out of proinsulin — it is measured to assess the body’s own secretion in patients on injections. In the granules insulin is stored as zinc hexamers.

Secretion

  • Glucose → GLUT2 (in humans mostly GLUT1) → glucokinase (sensor) → ATP/ADP ↑ → closure of K-ATP channels → depolarization → voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels → exocytosis.
  • Enhanced by: the incretins GLP-1 and GIP (cAMP), amino acids, parasympathetic nerves; inhibited by: epinephrine (α₂), somatostatin.
  • Two phases: rapid (ready granules at the membrane) and slow.

Action

Receptor tyrosine kinase → IRS → PI3K → Akt: GLUT4 to the membrane of muscle and fat, synthesis of glycogen, fat and protein; inhibition of gluconeogenesis, glycogenolysis, lipolysis and ketogenesis. Glucagon, epinephrine, cortisol and GH are counter-regulatory hormones.

  • Type 1 — autoimmune destruction of β-cells, absolute insulin deficiency; risk of ketoacidosis.
  • Type 2 — insulin resistance + progressive β-cell failure; hyperosmolar state in the elderly.
  • Gestational, MODY (monogenic, e.g. glucokinase mutations), secondary.
  • Diagnosis: fasting glucose ≥ 7.0 mmol/L, 2 hours after a glucose load ≥ 11.1, HbA1c ≥ 6.5%.
  • Complications: microangiopathy (retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy), macroangiopathy, diabetic foot.

\n <div><h2>Половые гормоны</h2>\n:
Sex hormones

Androgens (C19): testosterone, dihydrotestosterone, androstenedione, DHEA (mostly from the adrenals). Estrogens (C18, aromatic ring A): estradiol, estrone, estriol (from the placenta in pregnancy). In blood they are bound to sex hormone–binding globulin (SHBG) and albumin. They act through nuclear receptors (AR, ERα/β, PR): the hormone–receptor complex binds DNA and changes transcription. A mutation of the androgen receptor causes androgen insensitivity syndrome.

Regulation

  • Pulsatile GnRH → LH, FSH; continuous GnRH suppresses them (GnRH analogs in prostate cancer, endometriosis, precocious puberty).

hCG

A glycoprotein of an α subunit (shared with LH, FSH, TSH) and a β subunit (its own — this is what tests detect). It maintains the corpus luteum and, in a male fetus, stimulates Leydig cells.

A chromoprotein: the protein globin + 4 hemes. Normal range: 130–160 g/L in men, 120–140 g/L in women. Forms: HbA (α₂β₂, 97%), HbA₂ (α₂δ₂), fetal HbF (α₂γ₂). Neutrophils attack the crystals, and overnight an attack of intense inflammation develops — most often in the joint of the big toe. Under a polarizing microscope the crystals show negative birefringence; in chronic gout nodules (tophi) form. In detail — the “Nucleotides and gout” topic.
<b>Шаровидный сустав</b> — шаровидная го: A ball-and-socket joint — a spherical head in a socket: movement around three axes (flexion–extension, abduction–adduction, rotation) and circumduction. The shoulder joint is the most mobile in the body (the socket is shallow), and so it dislocates most often. The hip has its head deep in the acetabulum: it is stronger and more stable, but less mobile.
<b>Мыщелковый сустав</b> — два округлых: A condylar joint — two rounded condyles on almost flat facets: the main movement is flexion–extension, and when flexed some rotation is possible (two axes). The main example is the knee, the largest joint in the body; its surfaces do not match, so cartilaginous menisci lie between them, and cruciate ligaments inside. The temporomandibular joint is also condylar.

Bones

An adult has 206 bones: the axial skeleton (skull, spine, ribs, sternum) and the appendicular skeleton (girdles and free limbs). By shape — long, short (spongy), flat, irregular; sesamoid bones lie in tendons (patella).

  • Cells: osteoblasts build, osteocytes monitor, osteoclasts resorb; bone is remodeled throughout life (≈10% of the skeleton a year).
  • Growth in length — at the epiphyseal plate (cartilage), in thickness — from the periosteum.
  • Bone marrow: red — blood-forming, yellow — fatty.

Joints between bones

  • Fibrous: skull sutures, syndesmoses, gomphoses (teeth).
  • Cartilaginous: intervertebral discs, pubic symphysis, growth plates.
  • Synovial (joints proper): cartilage, cavity with fluid, synovial membrane, capsule, ligaments; sometimes discs and menisci.

Joint types by shape

Uniaxial — hinge, pivot; biaxial — ellipsoid, saddle, condylar; multiaxial — ball-and-socket; plane — small gliding movements in different directions.
